When women report sexual assaults, they generally expect law enforcement to investigate their allegations. Journalist Rae de Leon discovered a disturbing pattern in which some complainants instead found themselves accused of making false reports. Its most infuriating moments expose how easily the pursuit of justice can become another source of harm.

Working alongside the director and a drama therapist, the men recreate experiences from their past, using performance to confront painful memories and challenge the institutions that failed to protect them.

The resulting documentary is profoundly moving because its subjects actively shape how their experiences are represented. Rather than asking survivors to repeatedly recount their trauma for the camera, Greene allows them to participate in reconstructing their stories. It's a striking contrast to documentaries in which filmmakers struggle to establish the truth. Here, the camera becomes a means of reclaiming control over experiences that were once deliberately concealed.

Ari Folman's extraordinary animated documentary begins with a troubling realization: the Israeli filmmaker cannot properly remember his experiences during the 1982 Lebanon War. Hoping to understand what happened, he begins interviewing former comrades and reconstructing memories that have remained inaccessible for decades. Their recollections gradually lead toward the atrocities surrounding the Sabra and Shatila massacre.

Animation gives Waltz with Bashir an extraordinary visual identity, allowing Folman to explore dreams and fragmented recollections in ways conventional documentary footage could never achieve. As demonstrated by other animated movies based on true stories, the medium can reveal emotional experiences that resist straightforward representation. Folman's film goes further, confronting the possibility that memory itself can become an unreliable narrator. Its devastating conclusion leaves viewers questioning how much anyone can truly know about their own past.
